(p-٣٧٠) Surat al-Tariq (The Night-Comer)

Its purpose is to demonstrate the glory of the Qur'an in its truthfulness in reporting the bliss of the people of faith and the punishment of the people of disbelief on the Day of Resurrection, when the inner secrets are tested and the hidden consciences are exposed (al-Dama'ir), concerning the weight of an atom and what is less than that, all of which the noble recording angels have recorded in the scrolls of deeds, after the appointed terms have been fulfilled, as it was decreed from eternity without haste, and without delay beyond the set time or neglect. Its name, al-Tariq, is the clearest indication of this promised true reality when one reflects on the oath and what it is sworn to, according to how the discourse is arranged. (In the name of Allah) to whom all perfection belongs, (the Most Gracious) whose grace and justice encompass all creatures, (the Most Merciful) who singled out His friends with His success, so that His generosity, His kindness, His bounty and His favour became manifest to them.

* *

As was mentioned previously at the end of Surat al-Buruj, that the Qur'an is in a Preserved Tablet, because its place of descent encompasses the hosts of opponents and everything else, here it informs that part of its encompassing is the preservation of every single creature among all creatures, the opponents, the supporters and the allies, (p-٣٧١) so that they may be recompensed for their deeds on the day when realities are established and all ties are severed. He said, swearing to this because of their denial of it: ﴿By the sky﴾, that is, the sky possessing the stars placed to guard it from the rebellious devils, for the sake of preserving the glorious Qur'an, which guards the path of truth. Al-Malawi said: the intended meaning here is the spheres that revolve, not the highest heavens, [by means of] what He placed in them of night and day, and their rotation is three hundred and sixty degrees which never change, in this world, by a shortfall or an excess of even half a degree, nor a minute, nor a second, nor anything less than that; rather, whenever one of them increases by something, the other decreases by a corresponding amount. This is known from reason, transmitted reports and experience, so one knows that He who preserves is living and never dies, self-subsisting, who neither slumbers nor sleeps. End of quotation.

Since He swore by the sky because of its nobility and glory, alerting to the wonders of craftsmanship within it that point to overwhelming power, He swore by the most wondrous thing in it, namely the class of stars, and then by the most notable of them, the one appointed for guarding, as an alert to the marvels of power contained in that. He said: ﴿And by the Night-Comer﴾, that is, the class of stars that appears at night and is hidden by day, and which strikes (yatruqu) the eavesdroppers, scattering their assembly and destroying whomever Allah wills among them, for the sake of guiding people by the Qur'an along the spiritual paths, and its appearance and shining in the sky for guiding them along the sensory paths. Originally it refers to the traveller on the road (p-٣٧٢), and by convention it became specific to one who arrives at night, because he finds the doors closed and needs to knock on them (taraqa). Then the term was used for anything that appears in it, such as a star.

Since "al-Tariq" is applied to other things besides the star, He first made it ambiguous, then magnified the one by whom He swears with His words: ﴿And what can make you know what the Tariq is?﴾ That is, "Let Me inform you, O most noble of Our creation, upon him be blessings and peace, even if you were to try to know that and exert yourself greatly in searching for it: ﴿What is the Tariq?﴾"

Then He increased its awe by explaining it, after its vagueness, a second time with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The piercing star﴾, i.e., the one that blazes, is high and shines, as if it pierces the darkness with its light so that it penetrates it. It is said: "Pierce (athqib) your fire for the one who kindles," or it pierces the spheres with its light so that they become transparent to it, or the devil is pierced by its fire when he eavesdrops. The intended meaning is the genus, or a specific one known for piercing, which is Saturn. He first referred to it with a general description, then explained it with what is specific to it, magnifying its status because of the loftiness of its place.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 86, verse 4:

When he had mentioned that by which He indicated the preservation of the Qur'an from distortion, and the preservation of man, he mentioned its answer (jawab) concerning the preservation of the souls in which He placed the capacity to preserve the Qur'an in their breasts. He also indicated the preservation of what He created for their sake from these sworn-by things, which indicates the preservation of man. For if these things are preserved from the least deviation, while they were created to manage his interests, then what is to be assumed about him? So He said, emphasizing to the utmost degree (ghayat al-ta'kid), in response to what the disbelievers have of denial of that and of attack upon it (p. 373):

﴿Inna﴾, pronounced with the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah) in the recitation of the majority (al-Jumhur), meaning: indeed the matter is that ﴿every soul﴾, that is, of souls absolutely, and especially the souls of people, ﴿has over it﴾, that is, specifically over it, with none sharing with it in its essence, ﴿a guardian﴾, that is, a watchful, ready observer who does not part from it. By this is meant the category of angels. Some of them guard it from calamities, some guard it from whisperings (wasawis), some guard its deeds and count them by writing, and some guard what has been written for it of provision, term of life, wretchedness or happiness, walking, marriage, travel and residence, so that none of those things is transgressed. We have apportioned, We have decreed.

If you say: the guardian is the angels, you are right; and if you say: it is Allah, you are right, because He is the one who commands them and who empowers them for the guarding, and the guardian of them from weakness and deviation. So He is the true Guardian. The lam in this recitation is the one that distinguishes (al-fariqah) between the lightened form and the negating (nafiyah) particle. The ﴿mā﴾ is emphatic, negating the opening of what the sentence affirmed. ﴿Ḥāfiẓ﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾, and it is permissible for the adverbial phrase to be the predicate, with ﴿ḥāfiẓ﴾ raised by it.

Ibn ʿAmir, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read ﴿lammā﴾ with the doubled mīm, taking it to mean "illā" (except), and ﴿in﴾ as a negating particle meaning "mā." The excepted element (al-mustathnā minhu) is ﴿every soul﴾, and the predicate of the negating particle is omitted, its estimated form being: existing or present, or something similar. The excepted element is "a soul" described by "over which is a guardian," and it is possible that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), so its place (maḥall) may be in the nominative, being the predicate of the negator in this exceptive construction lacking its object (al-istithnā' al-mufarragh) according to the Banu Tamim, or in the accusative, being the predicate according to others. Or it may be a circumstantial clause from "nafs," because it is general. The sense is: no soul exists except a soul being, or being one over which there is a guardian.

The relation between the two recitations' implications is that the doubled form is more specific (akhass), because it is a perpetual absolute proposition (daʾimah muṭlaqah), whereas the lightened form is a general absolute proposition (muṭlaqah ʿāmmah). Let no one suppose that the doubled form is not equivalent to the lightened form, let alone that it is more specific. This is because the negating particle entered upon "kull" (every), which is among the walls of particular negation (aswar al-salb al-juz'i), as has been established in its place. So it resolves into: some souls are not except that over them is a guardian. He supposed that this is not so because it resolves, owing to the restriction it contains, which includes negation and affirmation, into two propositions: one affirming the guarding for the described soul, and the other removing its contrary from it, because restricting the described to the description is what is meant.

The contradictory (naqīd) of the universal affirmative is the particular negative, that is: it is not the case that every soul has over it a guardian. The particular negative is more general than the universal negative. So when you negate it, you say: "it is not the case that it is not the case that every soul has over it a guardian," and this is the negation of the particular negative. When it negates the particular negative, it negates the universal, because it has become clear that it is lighter. When the more general is negated, the more specific is negated, so no soul is such that there is not over it a guardian. The statement resolves into: no soul exists except a soul over which there is a guardian. Although the phrase "it is not the case that every" is among the walls of particularity as stated before, the verse in the doubled recitation becomes composed of an absolute general proposition, namely "every soul has over it a guardian" in actuality. Whoever negates its contradictory, which is the perpetual absolute proposition, that is "perpetually it is not the case that every soul has over it a guardian," and raises it by saying: "it is not perpetually that every soul is one over which there is no guardian," meaning, by way of restriction and limiting the described to the description, that the described does not exceed the description to which it is restricted. So at the least, it does not go beyond it to the absence of guarding. That is the meaning of the perpetual absolute proposition, which is the judgment that the predicate belongs to the subject so long as the subject exists. In the lightened recitation it is an absolute general proposition, meaning it is judged that the predicate belongs to the subject in actuality, and this is the first component of what the doubled recitation resolves into. So the implication of the verse in the doubled recitation is more specific than in the lightened recitation, because every perpetual is actual, but not conversely. This holds when we consider the concept derived from the wording itself apart from external indication. As for considering the reality itself, the aspect of perpetuity is the same, though the doubled recitation indicates it by the wording while the lightened does not. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said: Because Allah, glorified and exalted, said in Surah al-Buruj: ﴿And Allah is, over everything, Witness﴾ [al-Buruj: 9] and ﴿And Allah, from behind them, is Encompassing﴾ [al-Buruj: 20]. This contained an informing of the servants that He, glorified and exalted, nothing is hidden from Him, nothing escapes Him, and no fleeing one escapes from Him. He followed that with a detail that increases the clarification of that general informing, from His witnessing, glorified and exalted, over everything and His encompassing of it. So He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, informed of the particulars of every soul, from among those who guard its breaths: ﴿No word does he utter but that with him is a watchful observer ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], so that the servant knows that he is not neglected or wasted. He, glorified and exalted, is free of need for the records of the guardians and their counting, and the testimony of witnesses from the limbs and others. This was only for the manifestation of His justice, glorified and exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], and not less than an atom's weight. Rather, this is His practice, so that no one has any argument or pretext. He, glorified and exalted, swore to this, affirming and emphasizing it in a manner suited to the stated purpose. Ended.

Since the implied sense is: he must be presented before the Creator, glorified and exalted, for the assignment of guardians over a human being is only for presenting his deeds to the King, the Judge of Judgment, the Lord of command and proof, and calling him to account for what he did, the implied sense is: [the guardians] preserve his deeds (p-٣٧٧) and record them, so that the King may call them to account for that. Thereupon follows His statement, exalted is He: ﴿let man look﴾, i.e. with insight, ﴿man﴾, i.e. the one who is familiar with his own self, who examines his own inclination to see whether he is walking that path, ﴿from what﴾, i.e. from what thing, ﴿he was created﴾. The verb governing [من], the passive form, is built for the object, to inform that what indicates is the bare fact of creation, and as a reminder of the greatness of the Agent, since knowledge of Him does not need to be stated by name, for no one other than Him can produce any of His works. He commanded man to this kind of looking so that he would know, from the matter of his origin, the matter of his return. For whoever is able to originate is certainly able to restore. When this becomes sound in his mind, he strives not to dictate to his two recorders except what pleases God, exalted is He, on the day he is presented before the King, the Judge of Judgment, so that his reckoning will be easy for him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 86, verse 6:

When He had alerted (the reader) by the interrogative that this is a matter of great importance, such that every person ought to abandon all of his concerns and devote himself to reflecting upon it, for it earns him eternal, everlasting happiness, and since man, despite being weak and powerless, is never free from some preoccupation or lethargy, so that it is hardly possible for him to reflect properly, may He be glorified and exalted, undertook to explain this for him. He answered the interrogative with His saying: ﴿Created﴾, i.e., man was created in the easiest and simplest manner, after the creation of his father Adam, peace be upon him, from dust, and his mother Eve, peace be upon her, from his rib, ﴿from a gushing fluid﴾. That is: it (the fluid) is, due to the strength of nature's emission of it, (p-378) as if it gushes forth by itself; so this is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), while the gushing belongs to its possessor. Or it is a mathal (a form in which the attribute is expressed as though it were the thing itself), meaning "lāibn" (possessor of), i.e., one with a gushing, and "dafq" is pouring with propulsion in it. He did not say "two waters," indicating that the two (fluids) come together in the womb [and] mix with the utmost mixing, such that they become one water.

Since the intended meaning is the water of the man and the water of the woman, He said: ﴿it comes forth﴾. Some [read it] with the preposition affirmed, so it conveys the emergence from its place by His words: ﴿from between the backbone﴾, that is, the backbone of the man, which is a bone composed of joined vertebrae (mufallakah), whose binding is made as firm as possible, from the base of the neck to the coccyx; ﴿and the ribs﴾, that is, the ribs of the woman, which are the bones of the chest where the necklace rests. Ibn Jarir (Ibn Jarir al-Tabari) preferred this view. Or [the ribs are] what lies beside the two collarbones (tarquwah) of it, or what lies between the two breasts and the collarbones, [or - ] four ribs on the right side of the chest and four on its left side, or the two hands, the two feet, and the two eyes. In every case, her desire comes from in front of her, and the man's desire is in what is hidden from him behind him. Had He removed the preposition, it would have conveyed that the water fills the space mentioned, but it would not have conveyed that it comes out from the two sides of the space.

Al-Baydawi said: "Even if it is established that the drop (nutfah) is generated (yatawallad) from the surplus of the fourth digestion (al-hadm al-rabi') and separates from all the organs, so that it becomes ready for those same organs to be generated from it, its seat is a network of veins interlaced with one another near the two testicles. There is no doubt that the brain is the greatest of the organs in assisting its generation. For this reason it resembles the brain, and excessive intercourse quickly weakens the brain. The brain has a substitute, the spinal cord (al-nukha'), which lies in the backbone, and many branches descending to the ribs. These two are closest to the vessels of semen, and so they were singled out for mention."

Al-Mulawi said: "The One who brought it forth from the vessels of the bones of the backbone and the ribs, until He placed it in its locus between the two testicles, until it gushed forth, and then took care, after that, to transfer it from one creation to another every forty days, until He made it a human being who understands, speaks, builds palaces, and breaks rocks, is capable of resurrecting him."

When he knew, through the preservation and the creation in the stages referred to, that man was created for a great matter, namely the reckoning, and it was established that He has power to originate him from this water and to develop him through the states referred to by the mention of water, which are known to everyone, then the power to restore him is likewise established, with no difference except that restoration in the manner we know is easier. The Arabs used to deny it. He said, emphasizing, as a resumptive statement (istinaf) addressing one who says: "I have considered this, so, fa-mah," ﴿Indeed He, over his return, is able﴾. That is, the Creator of him, who is able to do what He has mentioned of his affairs, whose greatness is indicated by the passive form of khuliqa (the verb "was created"), ﴿over his return﴾, that is, the return of the human being to dust and his restoration to his first state and first creation as he was before death, and over the return of this gushing fluid to the channels from which it emerged, and its dissolution back into a watery state after it had formed into bone, flesh and blood. ﴿Is able﴾, that is, His power for that is firmly established with the utmost certainty. Thus, among the easiest things for Him, glorified and exalted is He, [His return - ] of a person after his old age to his beginning, by making him a middle-aged man, then a youth, then a child, then a clot of flesh, then a clinging clot, then a drop of semen, then He returns it to the male's sperm and the woman's womb, then to the man's loins and the woman's ribcage (tara'ib). That is easier for Him, and it is like His power to return him by resurrection. He expressed it with "innahu" (Indeed He) and did not say "Allah," for example, because it is more fitting, since it is said to every person: "Who brought you out in this form and made you this way?" So when He is described as the One who is able over everything with His complete power, it is said to him: "With that same power He will restore you." Had He named Himself by a name other than the pronoun, perhaps he would have said: "He is not my Creator."

Since this strongly stirs the listener to ask, "When will that return happen?", He answered him, saying: ﴿On the day when the secrets are tested﴾. The verb is put in the passive form (tubla) as an indication, together with a reminder of the ease of the matter, that it is among the clearest of matters, to the utmost clarity, that the One who tests them (p-381) is the One who returns them, namely God, glory be to Him, without any need to mention Him. ﴿The secrets﴾: that is, everything the breasts harbor of beliefs and intentions, and everything the limbs conceal of neglect in ablution, ritual bathing, and the like, of all sins. On that day, which is the Day of Resurrection, there will be among the awesome matters that which mixes with the secrets and turns them away from what they were, so they become manifest after having been hidden. Thus the good is distinguished from its bad, and its owner is recompensed for it.

Since the one who would prevent his requital, when his inner secrets are made manifest, is either himself or someone who helps him, He said, as a consequence of the manifestation of what he strives to conceal: ﴿Then he will have no power﴾, i.e., the human being whose secrets have been brought forth. He intensified the generality and negation, saying: ﴿of strength﴾, i.e., by which he could protect himself from the requital, ﴿nor any helper﴾, i.e., one who would help him and thereby prevent the execution of the judgment against him. Repulsion (dafʿ) is only by these two matters: a strength residing in him, or a strength external to him.

When these sentences, despite their brevity, comprised the highest summit of eloquence in establishing the resurrection (al-ba'th), the recompense, and His oneness, may He be exalted, along with other seas of knowledge, it was established that the Qur'an is the speech of God, may He be exalted, and it was established that (p-382) everything in it is true, despite their disputing all of that [entirely]. The circumstance required the oath to be sworn on its reality, so He said: ﴿By the sky﴾, that is, the one through which the oath was sworn at the outset, and He described it with what confirms the knowledge of al-'abath, which is the source of knowledge and piety, and upon which the foundation of happiness rests. So He said: ﴿that returns﴾, which returns by its rotation to the point from which it began its rotation. Thus return the states that passed and ended of the night and day, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the seasons: winter with its cold and rain, and summer with its heat, clarity, and stillness, and other things. And the plants return after they have crumbled and become dust mixed with the earth's dust. And the water returns, according to the view of those who say that the clouds take it from the sea, raise it up, press it out in the air, and then send it back to the earth, and other matters, each of which is a separate proof that the One who does that is able to restore everything that has perished, just as it was, without any difference at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 86, verse 12:

Having mentioned the heavenly matter first, because of its nobility, he followed it with the lower (earthly) matter, and God the Exalted said: ﴿And the earth﴾, that is, your dwelling, which you are constantly engaged with, dwell upon, and in contact with at all times, ﴿having the cleft﴾, that is, which splits open and cracks so that plants and springs come forth from it (p-383), as a clear proof of the beginning and the return (of creation) and of the resurrection. Thus, by the oath, he combined the upper world, which is like the man, and the lower world, which is like the woman. Just as the man waters her with his water so that she splits open [for the child], so the sky waters the earth so that it splits open [for the plants]. And just as it splits open for the plants, [so after their perishing and becoming crumbled dust, it returns them as they were,] so it splits open for people after their perishing, and they return as they were, by the permission of their Lord, with no difference at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 86, verse 13:

Since all of these are decisive proofs and dazzling, radiant indications of the truth of the Qur'an and of its coming with the highest eloquence, it was extremely far-fetched that they would slander the Qur'an after this clarity. God, the Exalted, said, alerting to that by emphasis, expressing by the pronoun as an indication of what has passed, that He is the one being spoken of now, so He is the one firmly fixed in all minds, with no absence [from him] of anything of them at all: ﴿Indeed, it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, which reported these reports that are in the utmost clarity, and it has preceded that it is glorious and in a Preserved Tablet, and that the disbelievers are in denial of it, especially what it includes of the report of the Resurrection: ﴿is indeed a decisive word﴾, i.e., very much, by which the separation of matters is intended, and it has such stature in distinguishing truth from falsehood that it has come to be called by the very name of "separation" (faṣl).

Then he emphasized the matter further because of the intensity of their denial, their repudiation, and their covering the truth with falsehood, so he said: ﴿And it is not﴾ (p-384) — that is, the Qur'an, in its inner and [not - ] outer aspects — ﴿with jest﴾, that is, with what is weak and despised, that has no benefit in it. Rather, it is right for it to be what it is now: awe-inspiring in hearts and exalted in breasts, such that its reciter and its listener are elevated above [indulging - ] in jest, and above being known for it in the eyes of the common people and the elite.

Since the persistence of this (matter) in this manner necessarily entails their eventual return from obstinacy, [that was what stirred the listener to seek to know what their situation had been. So He resumed His speech, indicating that they remained in denial, and emphasized it as a warning that their persistence in obstinacy] — despite this — is extremely unlikely. ﴿Indeed they﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿are plotting a plot﴾, i.e., with the stratagems they devise regarding his affair, ﴿a plot﴾ aimed at nullifying it and extinguishing its light by having you confirmed (in prison), or expelled, or killed, or by turning people away from you, while in fact they have no power at all to do so and no helper of any kind. The recompense He gives them, glory be to Him, is called a plot by way of mushakalah (verbal correspondence), and also because it is hidden from them and disagreeable to them, so it takes the form of a plot. Thus He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 86, verse 16:

﴿And I plan a plan﴾, i.e., I, by completing My power, ﴿a plan﴾ by drawing them on little by little (istidraj) to their deep immersion in what angers Me, so that there is completed that which necessitates My seizing them from where they do not perceive.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 86, verse 17:

When this indicated that they are nothing of account, He said, making it a consequence of that, as a threat to them (what a dreadful threat, how severe it is): ﴿So give respite﴾, meaning a great respite, by gradual steps. Since among those who deny, in God's knowledge, there are some who will believe, it is not fitting to inflict such a threat on them all, so He expressed it with a descriptive form that implies firmness, saying: ﴿the disbelievers﴾. That is, do not invoke curses upon them and do not seek to hasten their destruction, for We do not hasten. Only one who fears missing out hastens punishment. It is related that al-Hajjaj had a prison made of marble and its floor of lead, so it changed with the changing of the times: in the heat it was like Hell (jahannam), and in the cold like Zamharir (the frozen extreme). One day he passed by it and they cried out for help, so he lowered his head toward them and said: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. Then the ground seized the legs of his horse, so he raised his gaze to the sky and said: "Glory be to You! Only one who fears missing out hastens punishment," and he departed at that very moment. Hastiness (ʿajalah), which is placing a thing at other than its most fitting time, is a deficiency, for one hastens only when the one being hastened upon is beyond his grip.

Since the form taf'il (intensive verbal form) may convey prolongation, He emphasized it with the bare verb, indicating that what is meant by the first is the granting of respite, even though its time is short, by gradual steps, so that the one granting respite may be reassured by this, and he will have great strength and a true resolve (p-386), because what they say is something that souls strongly dislike, so no one can turn away from it except with great assistance: ﴿Give them respite﴾, that is, by turning away from them once, after the gradual steps which you were previously commanded to take, ﴿gradually﴾, that is, a slight respite. Soon there will be matters for them, and what matters will heal hearts. This is the diminutive of "irwadan," the diminutive of truncation (tasghir tarkhim). Ibn Burjan said: it is a word that gives gentleness. This latter sense is what is meant by what comes at its beginning, that each of them and others is preserved by His preservation, and their sayings, actions, movements, stillnesses and states are recorded, for that entails that they are within His grip. Thus the two parties met on the greatest matter with the clearest proof. The first of this threat occurred on the day of Badr, then their punishment, humiliation and abasement continued, until many of them were killed by the sword, and many died naturally and went to the Fire, while the rest remained in lowliness until God honored them with the honor of Islam, and they became among the great and eminent men, as an honor, dignity and exaltation for this noble Prophet, upon whom be the best of prayers and peace. And God, the Exalted, knows best what is correct.
